title: Why Won't My Water Heater Pilot Stay Lit?

seo.title: Why Won't My Water Heater Pilot Stay Lit?
seo.meta_description: A pilot light that will not stay lit can be caused by drafts, a failed thermocouple or sensor, a dirty pilot, gas control problems, or combustion issues.
seo.search_intent: Identify the most likely causes behind “Why Won't My Water Heater Pilot Stay Lit,” use distinguishing clues, and decide what to check first and when to get help.

excerpt: A pilot light that will not stay lit can be caused by drafts, a failed thermocouple or sensor, a dirty pilot, gas control problems, or combustion issues. Do not adjust gas valves or defeat safety devices. If you smell or hear leaking gas, leave the home without operating lights or phones and contact the gas utility or emergency services from outside.
content_html:
A pilot light that will not stay lit can be caused by drafts, a failed thermocouple or sensor, a dirty pilot, gas control problems, or combustion issues. Do not adjust gas valves or defeat safety devices. If you smell or hear leaking gas, leave the home without operating lights or phones and contact the gas utility or emergency services from outside.

If you smell gas, do not try relighting

Stop any relighting attempt and leave. Do not search for a leak with a flame or create sparks by operating switches. The priority is having the supply and appliance evaluated before returning or relighting.

Use only the manufacturer's lighting procedure

Some water heaters use electronic ignition while others have an accessible pilot control. Read the appliance label and follow waiting times. If the control will not hold the flame after the normal procedure, do not hold or block it in position.

A flame that dies when the control is released points to the safety circuit

A thermocouple or flame sensor confirms flame before continuous gas is allowed. Dirt, mispositioning, or failure can prevent that confirmation, but diagnosing or replacing gas components should follow manufacturer procedures and local requirements.

Repeated outages call for service

Venting, draft, gas control, or combustion may be involved. A water heater with soot, abnormal yellow flame, burning odor, or repeated pilot failure should remain out of service until checked by qualified personnel.

faq.question: What should I do if the pilot fails and I also smell gas?
faq.answer: Stop any relighting attempt and leave. Do not search for a leak with a flame or create sparks by operating switches. The priority is having the supply and appliance evaluated before returning or relighting.

faq.question: Can I hold the control down to keep the pilot lit?
faq.answer: Some water heaters use electronic ignition while others have an accessible pilot control. Read the appliance label and follow waiting times. If the control will not hold the flame after the normal procedure, do not hold or block it in position.

faq.question: What does it mean if the flame dies as soon as I release the control?
faq.answer: A thermocouple or flame sensor confirms flame before continuous gas is allowed. Dirt, mispositioning, or failure can prevent that confirmation, but diagnosing or replacing gas components should follow manufacturer procedures and local requirements.
